title: Itchy spots everywhere

clues.t: 4-year-old girl, fever and grumpy for a day.
Itchy red spots started on her chest and back.
New spots keep appearing in crops over 3 days.
Spots turn into small clear blisters, then crust over.
Some are in her mouth and on her scalp.
She hasn’t had the varicella vaccine.

pearl: Spots at different stages at once is the classic picture. Contagious until all are crusted. Avoid aspirin (Reye syndrome) and keep away from pregnant people and anyone with low immunity.

title: Itching all night

clues.t: 19-year-old student, intensely itchy for 4 weeks.
The itch is much worse at night.
His housemates are now itchy too.
Small bumps between his fingers and on his wrists.
Tiny wavy grey lines in the finger webs.
Skin scraping shows a mite and eggs.

pearl: Treat everyone in the household at the same time (permethrin cream, repeated in a week), and hot-wash bedding and clothes. The itch can last weeks after the mites are gone.

title: Breakbone fever

clues.t: 30-year-old woman, back from Bali 5 days ago.
High fever, severe headache and pain behind the eyes.
Aches in her muscles and joints.
A faint red rash with ‘islands of white’ on her legs.
Platelets 60 · white cells 2.8
NS1 antigen: positive

pearl: Watch for warning signs as the fever drops: tummy pain, vomiting, bleeding or drowsiness. Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin. A second infection with a different type can be more severe.

title: Changing mole

clues.t: 45-year-old man, his partner noticed a spot on his back.
He has fair skin and had many bad sunburns as a child.
The spot has grown over 6 months and itches.
It’s 9 mm with an irregular edge and several shades of brown and black.
It looks different from all his other moles: the ‘ugly duckling’.
Excision: atypical melanocytes invading the dermis, 1.2 mm thick

pearl: Australia has one of the highest melanoma rates in the world. Thickness (Breslow depth) is the key to prognosis. Sunscreen, shade and checking your skin save lives.

title: Fever after Africa

clues.t: 40-year-old man, home from visiting family in Nigeria 10 days ago.
He didn’t take any antimalarial tablets.
Fevers, chills and drenching sweats.
Now confused and slightly jaundiced.
Platelets 40 · lactate 4.5 · glucose 3.0
Thick and thin films: ring forms in 8% of red cells

pearl: Fever in a returned traveller is malaria until proven otherwise. Falciparum can kill within days; severe cases need IV artesunate. People who grew up in malaria areas lose their immunity after living away.

title: Rose spots

clues.t: 28-year-old woman, back from Pakistan 2 weeks ago.
A fever that has climbed higher each day for a week.
Headache, tummy pain and constipation.
Her pulse is 72 despite a temperature of 40 °C.
A few faint pink spots on her abdomen.
Blood culture: Salmonella Typhi

pearl: Treatment depends on resistance: many strains from South Asia are resistant to common antibiotics. Vaccination before travel helps but isn’t complete protection.

title: The ulcer that crept

clues.t: 63-year-old woman from the Mornington Peninsula, Victoria.
A painless lump on her calf that has slowly opened into an ulcer.
The ulcer’s edges are undermined: a probe slides under the skin.
Two courses of antibiotics for cellulitis didn’t help.
She feels well otherwise.
Swab PCR: Mycobacterium ulcerans

pearl: Called Bairnsdale ulcer in Victoria and Daintree ulcer in Queensland. Possums and mosquitoes are thought to play a part in spread. Treated with months of combination antibiotics, sometimes surgery.

title: Honey crusts

clues.t: 5-year-old boy, sores around his nose and mouth for 4 days.
They started after a cold with a runny nose.
Sores weep and form golden, honey-coloured crusts.
His little sister now has one on her chin.
He feels well and has no fever.
Swab grows Staphylococcus aureus.

pearl: Wash crusts gently and cover them. Small patches can be treated with antiseptic or antibiotic cream; widespread ones need tablets. Keep children home until treatment has started and sores are covered.

title: The whooping

clues.t: Mum brings her 7-week-old baby, who has had a cold for a week.
Now coughing fits so long his face goes red, then blue.
After one fit he paused breathing for 15 seconds.
Between coughs he looks surprisingly well.
His older brother has had a cough for a month.
Nose swab PCR: Bordetella pertussis

pearl: Very young babies may not whoop; they can stop breathing instead and need hospital. Vaccination in every pregnancy protects newborns. Antibiotics for the case and close contacts.

title: Sandpaper rash

clues.t: 6-year-old boy, sore throat and fever since yesterday.
A fine red rash spreading from his neck to his chest.
The rash feels like sandpaper.
Flushed cheeks with a pale ring around his mouth.
A red, bumpy ‘strawberry’ tongue.
Throat swab: group A streptococcus

pearl: Treat with penicillin to prevent complications such as rheumatic fever. Skin may peel on the hands and feet a week or two later.

title: Yellow after Thailand

clues.t: 26-year-old backpacker, returned from Thailand 4 weeks ago.
A week of nausea, fevers and feeling exhausted.
Now dark urine and pale stools.
His eyes have turned yellow.
ALT 1,850 U/L · bilirubin 90 µmol/L
Hepatitis A IgM: positive

pearl: Spread by contaminated food and water. Almost always gets better without treatment, and gives lifelong immunity. Two vaccine doses before travel prevent it; household contacts can be vaccinated after exposure.

title: Sunburn that isn’t

clues.t: 19-year-old woman, sudden high fever and vomiting.
Watery diarrhoea and muscle aches.
A red, sunburn-like rash all over her body.
BP 78/40; she’s confused.
She’s had a tampon in for 2 days.
Creatinine and liver tests rising; platelets falling

pearl: Remove any tampon or packing, give fluids and antibiotics including clindamycin to switch off toxin production. Skin on the hands and feet often peels 1 to 2 weeks later.

title: Locked jaw

clues.t: 70-year-old man, stood on a rusty garden stake 10 days ago.
He can’t open his mouth properly.
A fixed, grimacing smile.
His back arches with painful spasms when the door bangs.
He has never had a tetanus booster as an adult.
He is fully alert throughout.

pearl: Treatment: tetanus immunoglobulin, wound cleaning, antibiotics, muscle relaxants and often ICU. Having tetanus doesn’t give immunity: vaccinate afterwards.

title: The cheese lover’s fever

clues.t: 45-year-old man, fevers that come and go for 6 weeks.
Drenching night sweats with a strange smell.
Aches in his lower back and one knee.
He hunts feral pigs in Queensland.
His liver and spleen are slightly enlarged.
Blood culture (prolonged incubation): Brucella suis

pearl: In Australia, brucellosis is mostly caught from feral pigs. Overseas it comes from unpasteurised dairy. Treatment needs weeks of combined antibiotics to stop relapse. Warn the lab: it can infect lab staff.

title: After the holidays at the pool

clues.t: 14-year-old, swimming squad every day this summer.
Painful left ear for 3 days.
Pulling his earlobe makes it much worse.
The ear canal is red and swollen with white debris.
The eardrum looks normal once it can be seen.
Itchy before it became painful.

pearl: Clean the canal and use antibiotic–steroid ear drops. Keep the ear dry. Painful tug on the earlobe points to the canal, not the middle ear.

title: Cruise ship chaos

clues.t: 68-year-old woman on day 4 of a cruise.
Sudden vomiting started at 2am.
Watery diarrhoea followed within hours.
Dozens of passengers are sick with the same thing.
She’s mildly dehydrated but has no blood in her stool.
Stool PCR: norovirus

pearl: Hand sanitiser doesn’t reliably kill norovirus; soap and water does. Usually settles in 1 to 3 days. Stay home for 48 hours after symptoms stop.

title: Hot, swollen knee

clues.t: 72-year-old man with diabetes, right knee swollen since yesterday.
He can barely bend it and won’t put weight on it.
Fever 38.6 °C.
The knee is hot and red; any movement is very painful.
Joint fluid: cloudy, white cells 85,000
Gram stain: gram-positive cocci in clusters

pearl: A surgical emergency: a joint can be destroyed within days. Aspirate before antibiotics if possible. Gout can look identical, and the two can occur together.

title: Moving pain

clues.t: 17-year-old girl, tummy pain since last night.
It started around her belly button.
By morning it moved to her right lower abdomen.
She’s off her food and vomited once.
Pain gets worse with coughing and walking.
Ultrasound: thickened, non-compressible appendix

pearl: Pain that moves from the middle to the right lower abdomen is the classic story. In young women, also think of ovarian problems and ectopic pregnancy: do a pregnancy test.

title: The bird keeper

clues.t: 52-year-old woman, fever, headache and dry cough for a week.
Her chest X-ray shows patchy shadowing in one lung.
She didn’t improve on amoxicillin.
She breeds budgerigars; two died recently.
Her liver tests are mildly raised.
PCR on a throat swab: Chlamydia psittaci

pearl: Caught by breathing dust from bird droppings or feathers. Treated with doxycycline. Australian outbreaks have followed exposure to wild birds while mowing or gardening.

title: A kitten’s gift

clues.t: 10-year-old boy, a lump in his left armpit for 3 weeks.
It’s 3 cm, tender and slightly red.
He has a mild fever and feels tired.
His family got a new kitten last month.
A small healing scratch on his left hand.
Bartonella henselae serology: positive

pearl: Usually settles by itself over weeks to months. Kittens and young cats spread it most. Antibiotics are used for larger or more widespread cases.

title: Numb patches

clues.t: 33-year-old man, moved to Australia from India 5 years ago.
Pale patches on his back and arm for a year.
The patches feel numb to a pin and to heat.
He burnt his hand on a stove without noticing.
The nerve behind his elbow feels thick.
Skin smear: acid-fast bacilli

pearl: Curable with multidrug therapy, and not very contagious. Most people are naturally immune. Early treatment prevents disability; stigma, not the bacteria, is often the bigger problem.

title: Red and spreading

clues.t: 55-year-old man, painful swollen left lower leg for 2 days.
He has cracked skin between his toes from tinea.
The leg is red, warm and tender, with a fuzzy edge.
He has a mild fever.
The redness has spread past a pen line drawn yesterday.
Ultrasound: no clot

pearl: Treat the tinea too, or it may come back. Elevate the leg. Cellulitis is almost always one-sided: two red legs are usually something else, like venous eczema.

title: Winter wheeze in a baby

clues.t: 4-month-old baby, runny nose and cough for 3 days.
Now breathing fast and feeding only half her usual amount.
Her chest sucks in between the ribs with each breath.
Crackles and wheeze on both sides.
Her toddler brother had a cold last week.
Nose swab: respiratory syncytial virus

pearl: Treatment is support: feeding, fluids and oxygen if needed. Antibiotics, salbutamol and steroids don’t help. A vaccine in pregnancy and an antibody injection for babies now prevent many cases.

title: Chipmunk cheeks

clues.t: 22-year-old university student, feverish and tired.
Both sides of his face below the ears are swollen and sore.
Eating sour food makes it hurt more.
Several students in his dorm have the same thing.
A week later, his right testicle becomes painful and swollen.
Saliva PCR: mumps virus

pearl: Two MMR doses greatly reduce the risk. Outbreaks still happen in young adults. Testicular swelling occurs in about a third of men after puberty with mumps but rarely causes infertility.

title: Rash that won’t fade

clues.t: 17-year-old, felt fluey last night after a party.
This morning: high fever, vomiting and leg pains.
Cold hands and feet despite the fever.
Purple spots on her legs that don’t fade under a glass.
Now drowsy and confused.
Blood culture: gram-negative diplococci

pearl: Give antibiotics immediately; don’t wait for tests. Close contacts need preventive antibiotics. Vaccines cover the main strains, including B.

title: After the sore throat

clues.t: 12-year-old Aboriginal girl from a remote community.
Painful, swollen joints that move from knee to ankle to wrist.
Fever; she had a sore throat 3 weeks ago.
A new murmur at the apex.
ECG: PR interval prolonged
Anti-streptolysin O titre high

pearl: Australia has some of the world’s highest rates, mainly in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. Monthly benzathine penicillin injections for years prevent further attacks and heart damage.

title: Mosquito season in the Murray

clues.t: 48-year-old pig farm worker near the Murray River, after a wet summer.
Fever and headache for 4 days.
Now confused, with a tremor and stiff limbs.
He had a seizure on the way to hospital.
CSF: lymphocytes raised, protein raised, glucose normal
JEV IgM in CSF: positive

pearl: Spread by mosquitoes from pigs and wading birds. It reached south-eastern Australia in 2022. There’s no specific treatment, but a vaccine is available for people at risk.

title: Fevers every few weeks

clues.t: 19-year-old woman of Armenian background.
Since childhood, 2 to 3 days of fever every few weeks.
Each attack comes with severe tummy pain, once mistaken for appendicitis.
Sometimes painful swelling of one ankle with a red patch on the shin.
Between attacks she’s completely well; CRP very high during attacks.
Genetic test: two MEFV variants

pearl: Daily colchicine prevents attacks and the long-term risk of amyloidosis, which can damage the kidneys. Most common in people of Armenian, Turkish, Arab and Jewish ancestry. Today is Rare Disease Day.
